title: The Need for Material Metabolism Regulation in Closed-Loop Infrastructure
text:
The foundational legal structures governing urban construction and waste management were designed under a linear metabolic assumption, where material byproducts are classified solely as disposal burdens. The advent of closed-loop infrastructure design renders existing regulatory frameworks obsolete because they fail to establish a standardized 'resource substrate' value for industrial byproducts. Current permitting systems mandate disposal planning rather than systemic resource reclamation, creating economic disincentives against advanced circularity.

A crucial gap exists in governmental policy regarding the physical accountability of embedded material assets. To properly support closed loops, legal mandates are urgently needed to require comprehensive digital 'Material Passports' for major urban structures. These passports must track the chemical composition and potential re-use value of all components at the design stage, ensuring that future disassembly—not just disposal—is an economically viable outcome.

Furthermore, policy must shift from regulating material *input* to regulating functional *service life*. This necessitates legal frameworks that incentivize infrastructure designers to incorporate modularity and dematerialization plans throughout a product’s lifecycle, fundamentally altering the relationship between building codes, waste compliance, and long-term urban performance.
